Global Entrepreneurship Week: 37 founders’ ultimate tips for small business success

By Dan Martin
17 November 2026
0

    This week is Global Entrepreneurship Week. To celebrate, 37 entrepreneurs share their ultimate tips for small business success.

    Common small business success themes shared by the founders include:

    1. Know your numbers: Manage cash flow, understand profitability and price your products and services properly.
    2. Find your niche: Identify what makes your business different, understand your ideal customers and focus on the area where you can offer the greatest value.
    3. Put customers first: Listen to feedback, understand customer needs and build lasting relationships.
    4. Build strong networks: Seek mentors, collaborate and learn from other business owners.
    5. Keep adapting: Embrace change, innovation and continuous learning.
    6. Invest in people: Recruit well, delegate and empower your team to grow.
    7. Be resilient and confident: Take calculated risks, learn from mistakes and persevere through challenges.
    8. Market yourself consistently: Build visibility, communicate your value and invest in attracting customers.
    9. Look after yourself: Prioritise wellbeing, recognise your limits, ask for help and make time to step away from the business to avoid burnout.
    10. Define your own success: Focus on your goals, values and wellbeing rather than simply chasing growth.

    In full: The tips for small business success

    Don’t compare your day 5 to someone else’s year 5 – focus on you. It’s human nature to compare your success with others in your sector, but ‘comparisonitis’ is an affliction that can really damage your sense of achievement.

    Every journey is different and there’s no ‘one-size-fits-all’ to assure success. So, immerse yourself in learning the various tools and methods, learn from those who have already trodden the path, then choose the actions that feel aligned with your values, rather than doing what someone else said or trying to be more like them. Be more you!

    Rachel Haith, Inspired Life Group

    Grow your leaders, but never take your eye off the numbers. The best businesses don’t need their founder in every room. Build a clear path for the people closest to you to step up: teach them, trust them and give them real ownership.

    Every task you hand over frees you for the work only a founder can do. But handing over the doing never means handing over the knowing. Check your cash flow, and bookings every week, however busy things get. Invest in people, watch the numbers, and growth follows.

    Fi Da Silva-Adams, Revolution Performing Arts

    One of the biggest lessons I have learnt is that success comes from being prepared to adapt, embrace change and continually look for ways to improve.

    Build strong relationships, listen to your customers, surround yourself with good people and never be afraid to challenge the way things have always been done. You will not get everything right first time; but learn from every experience.

    Above all, believe in what you do, have the courage to take opportunities and never lose sight of why you started.

    Becky Wall, A Plush FLush and Loo of the Year Awards 

    Pay attention to where being needed is getting in the way of being effective. When you’ve built a business from scratch, being the person with every answer can become part of your identity. But if every decision needs your input, your availability sets the limit on what the business can achieve.

    Before concluding that your team needs to step up, ask what they’re waiting for: clarity, authority, or your approval? Building a successful business means allowing other people to become capable of things you’re used to being valued for.

    Alex Coward, leadership coach, business consultant and speaker

    Never be afraid to do things differently. I started my business during the pandemic, with three children at home and no grand business plan. I simply saw an opportunity where others saw a problem.

    We’ve built a business around rescuing and repairing furniture that might otherwise be discarded, proving that sustainability and commercial success can go hand in hand.

    But above all, stay adaptable. What worked yesterday might not work tomorrow. Listen, learn, change direction when necessary and never lose sight of why you started.

    Kirsty Allsopp, Gorgeous Little Things for Home

    know your numbers! If you leave your books until your tax return is due, you’re only doing them to keep HMRC happy, and by then the information is months out of date. Doing them in real time, ideally weekly but monthly at the very least, means you’ve got what you need to make confident business decisions now: whether you can afford to take on help, which products or services are making you money, whether your prices need to go up. Your numbers are there to help you, not just the taxman.

    Suzanne Brain, Small Business Bookkeeping (Stoke) Ltd

    In a small business, one hire can change how the whole team works. Yet most hiring decisions sit somewhere between gut feel and whatever’s in your head.

    For a while my business felt like Groundhog Day: a growth spurt, a key person leaving, delivery suffering, back to square one. What changed it was getting clear on where we were going, who we needed to get there and how we’d recognise them. Before your next hire, write those three things down. It turns a gut call into a decision you can repeat, and made a huge difference in my business.

    Sarah Ropek, The Fractional HR Department

    Early on, I spent too much time guessing what our tea drinkers wanted until I started emailing our most loyal buyers directly and jumping on quick video calls. I learned more about genuine buyer intent in a 10 minute chat than in months of looking at spreadsheets.

    My biggest advice is to regularly check in with your best customers, double down on what they love, and fix the things that frustrate them. They already hold the blueprint for your growth.

    Tatjana Anders, Teapro

    Don’t mistake starting again for starting from scratch. I’ve built a business, lost one and reinvented myself. The biggest lesson? Your experience never disappears. Your skills, relationships and even your mistakes become the foundations of what comes next. I’ve gone from building a design business to co-founding my current company with Em Burnip, working internationally in restorative travel and becoming an ambassador in Croatia.

    Success isn’t always a straight line, and it certainly isn’t always measured by this month’s profit. Sometimes the smartest business decision is having the courage to build something different with everything you’ve learned.

    Bex Hamilton, The Calm Travel Edit

    Do great work, and tell people about it.

    Which sounds simple enough; but when you’re growing and building a team it’s important to stay on top of quality – that’s what keeps people coming back.

    And when you’re busy, getting out there and blowing your own trumpet slides down the list until you’re quiet – and consistency beats sporadic every time.

    Owen Vittanuova, Paradigm

    Build your capacity, not just your business.

    Entrepreneurship demands resilience, adaptability and emotional intelligence, yet many business owners overlook the impact of chronic stress on their decision making, creativity and relationships.

    I’ve learnt that sustainable success isn’t about constantly pushing harder. It’s about recognising when to pause, regulate your nervous system and respond with clarity rather than react under pressure.

    A successful business should support your wellbeing, not come at the expense of it.

    Heidi Hadley, Total Somatics

    Stay lean and focus on profitability rather than vanity metrics. A growing turnover, bigger team or impressive client list doesn’t necessarily mean you’re building a healthier business.

    I prioritise sustainable growth, keeping overheads under control and investing in existing client relationships. Never underestimate the importance of proactive, honest communication, particularly when things aren’t going to plan. Retaining clients is far more valuable than constantly replacing them. Build a business that delivers genuine value, generates healthy profits and earns long-term trust.

    Damien Baxter, Geo Growth Media

    Always see yourself as a beginner. You might be an expert in your field, but you can still be an “expert beginner” who’s willing to ask questions, listen to fresh ideas and try a different way of working. That mindset keeps you humble enough to question what’s worked for years and curious enough to see what could work better today. The more experience you gain, the more valuable it is to keep that beginner’s curiosity.

    Andrew Wilkinson, Secure Safety Solutions

    For me, entrepreneurship starts with believing in an idea and having the courage to make it happen.

    My advice to aspiring entrepreneurs and SME owners is simple: know your purpose, understand your market and never compromise on quality or integrity. Build strong relationships, listen to your customers and surround yourself with people who share your ambition.

    Be prepared to take calculated risks and adapt to change. Keep a close eye on finances and never stop learning. Don’t wait for the perfect moment. Stay consistent and take action. Success is built on vision, resilience and the determination to keep moving forward.

    Rita W Bologna, serial entrepreneur

    Believe in your vision, even when others can’t see it yet. Building my business has taught me that success isn’t just about sales or profit. It’s about resilience, meaningful connections and the impact you make along the way. Not every day will be successful, and there will be moments when you question yourself, but consistency, authenticity and a willingness to keep learning are what move you forward.

    Surround yourself with people who encourage your growth, celebrate the small wins and never underestimate the power of simply showing up.

    Roxanne Clark, RoxEssential

    Business is not about guarding everything you know or seeing others in your industry as a threat. It’s about building relationships, sharing knowledge, supporting one another and recognising that we can achieve far more together than we ever could alone.

    Surround yourself with people who inspire you, celebrate others’ successes and never underestimate the value of a genuine connection. Some of the biggest opportunities come from conversations and collaborations you didn’t expect.

    There is room for everyone to succeed, and when we lift others up, we grow too.

    Emma Cartlich, Ultra Clean Canines

    Decide what success looks like for you, before you borrow someone else’s version of it. The internet will tell you to scale, hustle and build an empire, but plenty of us want a business that pays well, does good work and still leaves room for a life. That’s not settling, it’s designing.

    Get specific about the business and the life you want, then build towards that, and measure yourself against it, not anyone else. The most successful founders I know aren’t the biggest. They’re the ones building exactly what they set out to.

    Becky Benfield-Humberstone, quietly disruptive business coach and mentor

    In full: Tips for small business success

    I believe one of the biggest mistakes service-based businesses make is trying to appeal to everyone.

    When you’re a generalist, you’re often competing on price. However, when you become a recognised specialist, people seek you out for your expertise, not because you’re the cheapest. We chose to specialise in helping people overcome driving anxiety.

    It’s tempting to charge by the hour, but packaging your expertise into a premium programme, with a clear outcome and compelling value, can significantly increase what customers are willing to pay.

    My advice? Stop selling your time. Start selling your expertise and the transformation it delivers.

    Ian Murton, Ian Murton Hypnotherapy

    Realise that marketing and bringing in customers is not in addition to the work, it’s part of it. This is something you need to factor in time, energy and often money to master. You don’t need to like this, but you do need a way to keep helping people to find you, and you need to either build, borrow or buy your audience.

    All have their pros and cons, but you can’t skip this bit and expect a regular income. Get good at attracting clients!

    Laurie Macpherson, LinkedIn positioning strategist 

    Stop trying to be everything, all the time. Many of us believe we have to do it all ourselves to succeed, without realising how much that risks burnout. The most sustainable growth I’ve seen comes from getting unapologetically clear on how you work best: your energy, your focus, where you excel and what feels harder. Then build everything around that.

    For the things you find difficult, the answer is rarely to ‘just try harder’. It’s working out what support you need, whether that’s delegating, outsourcing or something more creative. Success doesn’t come from doing it all. It comes from alignment.

    Beth Thomas, CPD accredited professional speaker, trainer, recognised neurodiversity specialist and ADHD UK ambassador 

    Ask your customers plainly, why they struggle, then build everything around their answers.

    When my business was born, we started by asking small business owners why they don’t market more. Nearly every owner gave the same three reasons – not enough money, not enough time, and not knowing where to start.

    To this day, those three answers remain our filter. Before we build a feature or take on any task, we ask one question: does it solve all three? And if it doesn’t, we don’t build it.

    Focusing intently on our customers’ needs prevents us from over-complicating things.

    Joe Tompkinson, MyMarketr.io

    Charge more. No, more than that. When we started our business, I priced work for the client to accept because we really wanted to work with them. But clients anchor to your first price, and it’s very hard to move them up from there. So charge commercially from day one. And remember: the client who haggles on the proposal will haggle on every invoice.

    Adams Ginns, Layers Accountancy

    Put yourself out there for opportunities! Often opportunities don’t just land at your door, so don’t be afraid to put yourself forward.

    Make your own luck: pitch to your dream client, ask a mentor for help, and apply for the award. Even if you doubt yourself or the opportunity seems too big – say yes and figure out the details later! Every opportunity goes to someone; why not you?

    Maya Vertigans, Planner Bee VA Services

    Many capable business owners talk themselves out of brilliant ideas, not through a lack of ability, but because our brains are wired to protect us from risk, rejection and judgement. My tip is to lean into the fear, rather than avoid it.

    First, ask “What’s the worst that could happen?” and picture it. Second, ask “How would I cope?”; we often underestimate our ability to cope, and as we imagine handling it, fear loses its power. Third, take the first step as an experiment. Whatever the result, you gain insight, momentum and the self-trust to make bolder business decisions.

    Dr Rachel Lee, Born to Be Bold

    Understand your numbers, protect your cash flow and plan ahead. Too many business owners focus only on generating sales without keeping a close eye on the financial health of the business.

    Sustainable growth comes from making informed decisions, knowing when to invest and getting the right support at the right time. You don’t have to be the biggest business in your industry; you need to make smart, consistent decisions.

    Owen Guy, DNA Finance

    One of the biggest lessons I’ve learned from running my own business is to never stop investing in your marketing.

    You can be brilliant at what you do, but if nobody knows you exist, you’ll struggle to grow.

    One mistake I see small business owners make is only focusing on marketing when they need more customers. By then, they’re already playing catch-up.

    Make marketing a consistent part of your working week, even when you’re busy. You don’t need a huge budget, but you do need a plan that generates enquiries and helps turn them into paying customers.

    Emma Michael, Emma Michael AI Solutions

    My biggest tip for business success is knowing your numbers. It’s easy to get excited about how much money is coming in, but turnover means little if you don’t understand what’s going out. Get comfortable reading your profit and loss statement; know your monthly expenses and keep a close eye on cashflow.

    I see the same thing in property investment. A great rental yield might look impressive, but once you factor in mortgage payments, maintenance, void periods and other costs, the reality can be very different. Real success is less about what you earn and more about what you keep.

    Melissa Lewis, ML Property Venture

    Fix the owner before you fix the business.

    Your brain is a prediction machine, and it runs your company on forecasts built from old experiences, so if it predicts rejection, you’ll find yourself reorganising your inbox at 4pm instead of making the sales call

    Around 70% of people experience imposter feelings at some point, and in business owners it shows up as underpricing, overdelivering and avoiding the camera.

    You can’t strategise your way past a pattern your nervous system is running. Delete the pattern and the strategy you already had starts working.

    Krystyna Lennon, DELETE Method Academy

    Build your business around what you understand and what feels deeply aligned with your heart.

    Five years ago, I lost my husband. Energy healing and hypnotherapy carried me through my most difficult time.

    For years, my self-doubt kept me small until becoming a hypnotherapist healed my belief that I wasn’t worthy to help others.

    Two years ago, I answered my calling to support people through grief and trauma. I understand that the heart is where we create from, and carrying sadness makes it harder to find hope. Healing it lets us move forward

    Sangeeta Dewan, grief and trauma therapist

    Success starts with unwavering self-belief. You have to believe in your vision long before anyone else can see it. When I founded my business, my mission wasn’t simply to teach performing arts; it was to build confidence in children that would stay with them for life. That purpose has guided every decision as we’ve grown nationally. But growth also requires you to evolve as a leader.

    You cannot build an extraordinary business doing everything yourself. Surround yourself with brilliant people, trust them to deliver, and create the space to think bigger. Never underestimate what unwavering belief, purpose and determination can build.

    Zoe Harrison, ZLH Studios

    Most people quit a business, an idea, or a team too early — not because it wasn’t working, but because it wasn’t working fast enough.

    Great things aren’t built just in the good times, They’re built in the boring ones too! The ones where you keep showing up, keep improving, keep leading when no one is clapping!

    Patience isn’t sitting back and hoping for the best. It’s staying committed while the results catch up.

    At an early stage in my business, I was told to play the long game because most of your competition won’t. How true was that!

    John Lewis, JL Mindset Performance

    Deal with the difficult things early. If something doesn’t feel right, whether a client issue, a difficult conversation, or something in the business that simply isn’t working, don’t leave it hoping it’ll sort itself out. It rarely does.

    You won’t always have all the information, and you don’t always get every decision right, but dealing with things honestly and directly gives you a much better chance of fixing them.

    Be fair, listen to people, consider your options, then make the decision and move on. Putting off the difficult stuff nearly always makes it harder in the long run.

    Emma Carter, WestSpring IT

    Friends first, business second. What I’ve learned in my 17 years as a business owner is that the real magic happens when you surround yourself with people who genuinely want you to win.

    Focus on building genuine authentic relationships and the business will follow naturally afterwards. I highly recommend finding your tribe(s) – the ones who’ll cheer loudest for you, refer you without being asked and offer you support when you need it.

    If you give more than you take, not only will your business become more successful – it will enrich and enhance every aspect of your life too.

    Sarah Ridge, The Sisterhood Networking Group

    Don’t just build a business. Build a community. When I founded my business, I thought I was offering people a way to quit drinking. I soon discovered that what they really needed was connection, encouragement and a sense of belonging. That’s what transformed my business.

    My advice to entrepreneurs is to listen carefully to your customers, understand what they truly need and make them feel part of something bigger.

    Products can be copied. Genuine human connection can’t. Build trust, create belonging and your customers will become your greatest ambassadors.

    Janet Gourand, Tribe Sober

    Don’t try to do everything on your own. There’s a surprising amount of help available for small manufacturers, and many businesses don’t take advantage of it. Through the Made Smarter programme, our honey-brewed Jun kombucha business has received expert advice on how tech can help us grow. The programme has also funded an internship for a University of Brighton graduate with a master’s degree in user experience design who will help us improve how we manage orders and track our products.

    We’re also talking to other local brewers and manufacturers to share ideas, contacts and advice. Whether it’s government support, grants, universities or other businesses, there’s plenty of help out there, so use it.

    Robert Marchant, Pop Cultures kombucha

    Definitely listen to advice, and know your numbers inside out, but my best tip for business success is to trust your instincts. You will generally know the answer if you fully pay attention to yourself.

    Jenna Wilson, Little Dreams Consulting

    Learn to see everything as a learning experience.

    Every failure can increase your knowledge. Learning what NOT to do can be as useful as learning what you SHOULD be doing. Over the years I’ve screwed up countless times in ways that would make you wince. I’ve also done things that have left people saying `How did you think of that good idea?’

    When you preside over the proverbial ‘epic fail’, ask yourself ‘What’s the lesson I can take from this?’ and then act on it.

    Steven Wade, Family Law Assistance
